Our algorithm attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$ regret using only linear optimization oracles, and the near-optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret when an optimal-design exploration distribution is further available. This improves on the $T^{2/3}$ regret of the FTPL algorithm of Dani and Hayes (2006) for general action sets, and generalizes the $\sqrt{T}$ regret of Lévy et al. (2026) over two special action sets (hypercube and Euclidean ball). Compared to previous oracle-efficient linear bandit algorithms based on continuous exponential weights, the FTPL approach generally has better computational efficiency, and is much simpler to implement.
  The key algorithmic element is a perturbation distribution that adapts to the past reward estimators. Its simplest form, an adaptive Gaussian perturbation, is straightforward to implement and already attains the regret bound above. We further extend it to two general constructions, random-weighting and elliptical perturbations, each covering distributions from light tails (Gaussian) to heavy tails (Student-$t_2$). On the technical side, we develop a systematic way to analyze the stability term in the FTPL regret through the Fisher information of the perturbation distribution. This builds a general framework for FTPL beyond existing ones such as the hazard rate and the FTRL-FTPL duality.

Machine Learning.title: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
Machine Learning.summary: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open-weight configurations, multi-run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/manoharvellala/Hardeval The paper has 4 figure environments (two are images, two are the example-prompt panels) and 4 tables

Machine Learning.title: AceFF: A State-of-the-Art Machine Learning Potential for Small Molecules
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce AceFF, a pre-trained machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) optimized for small molecule drug discovery. While MLIPs have emerged as efficient alternatives to Density Functional Theory (DFT), generalizability across diverse chemical spaces remains difficult. AceFF addresses this by refining the TensorNet2 architecture and training it on a comprehensive dataset of drug-like compounds. This approach yields a force field that balances high-throughput inference speed with DFT-level accuracy. We introduce two models sharing the same architecture: \mbox{AceFF-2}, trained on our own dataset of small molecules and supporting the essential medicinal chemistry elements (H, B, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, Br, I); and \mbox{AceFF-2-OMOL}, trained on a subset of OMol25 containing the AceFF-2 elements plus the common biomolecular ion elements Na and K. The models are explicitly trained to handle charged states. Validation against rigorous benchmarks, including complex torsional energy scans, molecular dynamics trajectories, batched minimizations, and tests of force and energy accuracy, demonstrates that AceFF is state-of-the-art for organic molecules in the accuracy and speed regime important for drug discovery. The AceFF-2 and AceFF-2-OMol model weights and inference code are available at https://huggingface.co/Acellera/AceFF-2.0 and https://huggingface.co/Acellera/AceFF-2-OMOL.

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable experiential learning based on state history and global feedback
Machine Learning.summary: A new interpretable experiential learning model based on state history and global feedback is presented. It is capable of learning a behavioral model represented by a transition graph between sets of states, with transitions attributed with utility and evidence count. This model is expected to be suitable for solving reinforcement learning problem in resource-constrained environments. The model was thoroughly evaluated on the OpenAI Gym Atari Breakout benchmark, demonstrating performance comparable to some known neural network-based solutions.
Machine Learning.comment: 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Machine Learning.title: Learning to Reason About Implicit Multimodal Harm: From Diagnosis to Generalization
Machine Learning.summary: A benign image paired with a benign caption can become harmful only in combination, making detection fundamentally a cross-modal reasoning problem. Existing multimodal harm benchmarks evaluate only classification accuracy, leaving unclear whether models identify the cross-modal mechanism that produces harm. We introduce MuPHI (Multimodal Pragmatic Harm Interpretation), a controlled diagnostic benchmark in which harm arises purely from image-text composition, with benign counterfactuals and annotated harm rationales. Using MuPHI, we systematically evaluate where compositional harm reasoning breaks in vision-language models (VLMs). MuPHI reveals that VLMs reliably ground each modality yet fail to bind the evidence into the harm mechanism and their predictions respond weakly to label-determining counterfactual interventions. Moreover, existing harm detection approaches trained on labels substantially improves in-domain (ID) detection but transfers poorly across harm distributions. We therefore propose Compositional Harm Interpretation Learning (CHIL), which rewards evidence identification in each modality, cross-modal binding and verdict consistency in the reasoning chain rather than just predicted label. CHIL improves 81% OOD transfer evaluations by an average of +2.5 macro-F1 and correct counterfactual flip rate by up to +3.8 and +5.4 % points, while also improving overall reasoning quality over label-only optimization. These results suggest that optimizing how a model reasons, not just what it concludes, offers a promising direction for multimodal safety systems that generalize beyond dataset-specific correlations.

Machine Learning.title: TriRouter: Sparse-to-Dense Electrode-Space Routing for Robust EEG Motor Imagery Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Motor imagery brain-computer interfaces require reliable decoding from multichannel EEG, but practical acquisition often yields sparse or corrupted electrode montages. We propose TriRouter, an electrode-space routing framework with discriminative-preservation, mask-robustness, and latent-compensation paths. A validation-calibrated router uses observable channel availability to allocate path contributions, preserving complete-channel discrimination while increasing representation recovery under severe missingness. In BNCI2014-001, TriRouter outperforms standard public backbones and a dynamic-spatial-filtering corrupted-EEG baseline. It improves accuracy over the strongest corrupted-EEG baseline by 3.68, 4.02, and 6.46 percentage points at nominal 25%, 50%, and 75% missing settings, and remains effective under structured regional missingness and additional low-channel dataset evaluation.

Machine Learning.title: An Efficient Approach to Beetle Damage Detection of Banana Using Deep Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Visible surface damage of banana fruits by Basilepta subcostata (the banana fruit scarring beetle) can reduce their market value. Here, manual inspection of Banana fruits is subjective and difficult to scale. This study presents a lightweight framework based on YOLOv8n deep learning model for locating individual bananas and classifying their visible surface condition as healthy or unhealthy. The term beetle damage in the paper title is used operationally for the locally observed scar-like surface condition; the model does not identify a specific beetle species or biological cause. A custom dataset of 2,473 images containing 5,827 annotated banana instances was prepared from local-market imagery in Bangladesh. The reported experiment used an 80/20 protocol with 1,982 training images and 491 test images. A pretrained YOLOv8n model was trained at 640x640 resolution for 50 epochs with a batch size of 4. On the test partition, it achieved 81.36% precision, 74.30% recall, 77.67% F1-score, 87.04% mAP@0.50 and 59.33% mAP@0.50:0.95. A YOLOv8s comparison gave slightly lower F1 and mAP while using a substantially larger checkpoint. The YOLOv8n checkpoint occupied 5.96 MB and required 6.54 ms/image for inference on an NVIDIA Tesla T4. The results support YOLOv8n as a compact baseline for instance-level banana surface inspection within the studied acquisition conditions.
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages. Accepted at the 12th IEEE International Conference on Sustainable Technologies and Engineering (IEEE iCOSTE 2026), Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 1-3, 2026

Machine Learning.title: DisCo Algebra: Why Disintegration and Combination Are Not Inverses
Machine Learning.summary: We present DisCo algebra---a compositional framework for joint probability built from a symmetric cooperad (disintegration) and a non-unital partial symmetric operad (combination restricted to the image of disintegration) on the bare family $\mathcal{P}_n=\mathrm{Prob}([0,1]^n)$. No probability integral transform, no external summary functions, no enrichment of objects with conditional kernels. The disintegration side uses block-wise joint CDFs as intrinsic, measure-determined 1D summaries, yielding a lossy compression. The combination side reads the same summaries and reconstructs via regular conditional measures, yielding a lossless embedding on admissible inputs. We prove that combination followed by disintegration is the identity on admissible inputs, but disintegration followed by combination is not---it defines a renormalization operator $R_{\mathcal{I}}=\text{Combine}\circ\text{Disintegrate}$. The information loss of this operator is exactly the probability curvature $\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{I}}(μ)$---the conditional KL divergence between the true conditional distribution and the conditionally independent product. This curvature measures the obstruction to lossless decomposition and reveals a hard limit on how much cross-block dependence can be captured by CDF-based scalar block summaries.

Machine Learning.title: A Language-Informed Loss for Visual Generation
Machine Learning.summary: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 $\to$ 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.

Machine Learning.title: JAXtari: High-Throughput and Easy-to-Modify Arcade Learning Environment
Machine Learning.summary: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) has been a cornerstone of Deep Reinforcement Learning research, providing a standardized benchmark for evaluating general agents. However, its lack of native support for object-extraction and environment modification restricts research into evaluating whether agents learn robust causal models or rely on brittle visual heuristics. Furthermore, the ALE's dependence on CPU-based emulation creates a significant bottleneck in modern GPU-accelerated training pipelines, limiting both experimental scale and iteration frequency. In this work, we introduce JAXtari, an open-source, high-performance reimplementation of Atari 2600 environments. By leveraging massive GPU parallelization, JAXtari allows PPO agents to finish training on 100M environment steps on a single A100-GPU in under an hour. Beyond speed, it provides object-centric observations and a flexible modification system, allowing researchers to, e.g. develop neuro-symbolic methods or discover novel shortcuts and subsequently train and adapt their agents rapidly, sometimes in only minutes.

Machine Learning.title: Scalable long-range machine learning interatomic potentials with electrical response for atomistic material modeling
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate atomistic simulations of materials under electric fields require long-range electrostatics and electrical-response modeling at length scales beyond the reach of conventional first-principles methods. Yet these capabilities remain difficult to reconcile with the scalability of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Strictly local models enable efficient spatial parallelization but neglect long-range interactions, whereas existing electrostatic extensions introduce global dependencies that hinder distributed computation. Here, we overcome this limitation by analytically separating the long-range electrostatic forces and Born effective charges (BECs) into a global electrostatics calculation and strictly local derivatives of learned latent charges. This formulation preserves the spatial decomposability of equivariant MLIPs while enabling distributed evaluation of energies, forces, stresses, and BECs across different boundary conditions. Implemented as DPA4C-LR on the \texttt{nvalchemi} platform, the framework scales to 5.2 million atoms on four GPUs at approximately twice the computational cost of its short-range backbone. Trained on energies and forces, DPA4C-LR accurately infers BECs and reproduces the field-dependent infrared spectra of water. We further demonstrate its capabilities by recovering the characteristic slim polarization hysteresis of relaxor \ce{Pb(Mg_{1/3}Nb_{2/3})O3}, which is obscured by finite-size effects in smaller simulations; predicting a room-temperature field-driven ionic conductivity of $6.8 \pm 0.7$~mS/cm in amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}}; and modeling interfacial thermal transport across Si/diamond interfaces with slab-corrected electrostatics. By combining long-range physics, electrical-response inference, and distributed computation, this framework extends predictive atomistic modeling toward device-relevant length scales.

Machine Learning.title: No-Regret Mixing of LRU and LFU with Optimal Switching Cost
Machine Learning.summary: Caching systems often rely on simple eviction policies such as Least Recently Used (LRU) and Least Frequently Used (LFU), which perform well in complementary request regimes. Recent policies such as LeCar and Cacheus combine LRU and LFU using ideas from the experts problem in online learning. Specifically, upon a miss, they randomize between the two eviction rules using probabilities derived from scores updated by tracking the history of past evictions. While these policies exhibit strong empirical performance, it remains unclear whether they are guaranteed, on every request sequence, to perform asymptotically as well as the better of LRU and LFU, i.e., whether they achieve sublinear regret with respect to this benchmark. We first show that LeCar suffers linear regret against an oblivious adversary, even with unbounded history. We then propose H-MC, a Hedge-based mixture of virtual LRU and LFU caches that preserves Hedge's selection probabilities, and hence its regret guarantees, while minimizing the switching cost among all joint selection rules with these marginals.

Machine Learning.title: No-Regret Language Generation
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce no-regret generation, which requires a generator to make a sublinear number of mistakes uniformly over all demonstration sequences and compatible target languages. We also formulate an agnostic variant that allows arbitrary demonstrations that may not be compatible with any languages. For both settings, we introduce tree-based mistake-forcing dimensions that exactly characterize finite-horizon minimax complexity and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for no-regret generation. Our characterizations reveal a rich spectrum of generation rates: up to constant rescaling, every admissible nondecreasing profile is attainable in both the realizable and agnostic settings. Finally, we connect generation complexity to online prediction: for language classes of finite Littlestone dimension \(d\), we obtain realizable mistake bounds of \(O(d\log(1+T/d))\) and agnostic regret bounds of \(O(\sqrt{dT\log(1+T/d)})\). The realizable bound is optimal up to universal constants.

Machine Learning.title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading
Machine Learning.summary: In a previous report we showed that a decoder can recover open-vocabulary word-level information from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, by aligning short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model (LLM). That analysis contrasted two of the model's 33 layers: the context-free input embedding and one mid-depth layer. Here we ask how EEG-decodable structure is distributed over the full depth of the language model. We trained one decoder per layer of Llama-3.1-8B, with and without a causal transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. We distinguish word-level decodability from a context-tracking component. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines steadily towards the last layer. In contrast, the context-tracking component of the retrieval gain rises with depth, both with and without a causal transformer. Unexpectedly, a decoder that sees a single 0.5-s window at a time tracks the text passage too. Two new controls dissect this component. A target-geometry control, a synthetic predictor made of the true target plus noise calibrated to each decoder's word-level accuracy, shows that context tracking is not a by-product of word decoding and target geometry. A control that permutes predictions across runs from either the same or from different sessions shows that most of the observed context-tracking is not caused by an EEG recording session signature. Instead, context tracking mostly follows the text. A single EEG window therefore carries passage-level information that a contextual target can absorb. The results locate word identity in the early layers of the language model, discourse state in the deeper layers, and make the choice of target layer a design dial for EEG language decoders.
Machine Learning.comment: 41 pages (including 23 pages of Supplementary Material), 12 figures (including 5 in Supplementary Material)

Machine Learning.title: A New Family of Poisson Non-negative Matrix Factorization Methods Using the Shifted Log Link
Machine Learning.summary: Poisson non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is a widely used method to find interpretable "parts-based" decompositions of count data. While many variants of Poisson NMF exist, existing methods assume that the "parts" in the decomposition combine additively. This assumption may be natural in some settings, but not in others. Here we introduce Poisson NMF with the shifted-log link function to relax this assumption. The shifted-log link function has a single tuning parameter, and as this parameter varies the model changes from assuming that parts combine additively (i.e., standard Poisson NMF) to assuming that parts combine more multiplicatively. We provide an algorithm to fit this model by maximum likelihood, and also an approximation that substantially reduces computation time for large, sparse datasets (computations scale with the number of non-zero entries in the data matrix). We illustrate these new methods on a variety of real datasets. Our examples show how the choice of link function in Poisson NMF can substantively impact the results, and how in some settings the use of a shifted-log link function may improve interpretability compared with the standard, additive link.

Machine Learning.title: Deconstructing Multi-Task Active Learning: The Paradox of Gradient Conflict and Orthogonal Decomposition
Machine Learning.summary: Existing multi-task active learning (MTL-AL) methods predominantly rely on linear scalarization of heterogeneous objectives such as uncertainty, diversity, and gradient conflict. We argue that this entangled formulation is fundamentally limited, as linear combination fails to capture Pareto-optimal trade-offs under conflicting objectives. We propose a shift from combination to deconstruction and introduce a principled framework that rethinks MTL-AL along three orthogonal dimensions. First, we identify the Conflict Paradox: although the optimization literature treats gradient conflict as interference to be suppressed, penalizing conflict when ranking candidates is measurably worse than not scoring it at all. We therefore decouple the two concerns: the acquisition function does not score conflict, and the resulting interference is resolved by gradient surgery during training. Second, we introduce Orthogonal Decomposition, separating acquisition into Informativeness and Exploration. This two-stage process, informativeness filtering followed by coverage maximization, prevents "diversity dilution" by excluding uninformative outliers before enforcing diversity. Third, we propose Cross-Task Mutual Information (CTMI), a covariance-based statistic of cross-task dependency computed from MC-dropout task entropies. Extensive experiments on COCO, Cityscapes, and NYUv2, including comparisons against recent MTL-AL and data-selection baselines, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting that structural rethinking of acquisition yields larger gains than incremental heuristic design. Code is available at https://github.com/Juho-Jung/multitask_active_learning_official.

Machine Learning.title: Worst-Case Optimal $\sqrtε$-Rate Stability of KL Divergence under Perturbations of Gaussian Distributions
Machine Learning.summary: We establish a stability bound for the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence when its Gaussian reference distribution is perturbed. Existing relaxed triangle inequalities of KL divergence between Gaussian distributions require all three distributions to be Gaussian, which limits their use in applications such as out-of-distribution detection with flow-based generative models. Let $\mathcal{N}_1$ and $\mathcal{N}_2$ be $d$-dimensional Gaussian distributions, and let $P$ be any $d$-dimensional distribution satisfying $\mathbb{E}_P[\|X\|^2]<\infty$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P\Vert \mathcal{N}_1)<\infty$. If $\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}_1\Vert\mathcal{N}_2)\leqε$ for $0<ε<1/12$, we give an upper bound of $\left|\mathrm{KL}(P\Vert\mathcal{N}_1)-\mathrm{KL}(P\Vert\mathcal{N}_2)\right|$. Under suitable uniform boundedness conditions, the bound is $ \frac{\sqrt{6dε}}{2}+K\sqrtε+o(\sqrtε)$ as $ε\rightarrow 0$ for fixed $d$, where $K$ depends on the parameters of $\mathcal{N}_1$ and $\mathcal{N}_2$, and on $\mathbb{E}_P[\|X\|]$ and $\mathbb{E}_P[\|X\|^2]$. Furthermore, we prove that the $\sqrtε$ dependence is worst-case optimal. The result extends stability guarantees restricted to Gaussian triples to comparisons involving an arbitrary distribution and two nearby Gaussian references. Experiments on synthetic distributions and latent representations from flow-based models support the predicted stability behavior.

Machine Learning.title: GRAFT-EEG: Gauge-Aware Physical Field Transport for Cross-Dataset Motor-Imagery EEG
Machine Learning.summary: Cross-dataset EEG decoding often treats montage, reference, and active-sensor changes as representation shift, although they also alter the observation operator. We study target-statistics-blind transfer: fitting receives no target signal, label, or empirical statistic, and electrode coordinates only instantiate a fixed prediction operator. method removes the active-set common-reference gauge and transports each native mask through a template motor leadfield. A source-fitted spectral classifier anchors the decision; a bounded state-space-model (SSM) residual is secondary. We establish restricted identifiability and an operator-perturbation bound. Across five leave-one-dataset-out targets (253 participants), dynamic method achieved 60.865% equal-target balanced accuracy versus 52.684% for strict-clean 5/5 BIOT (hierarchical difference +8.182 points; 95% CI +6.382 to +10.196; positive in every target). On four EEGPT-clean targets, the descriptive means were 61.520% and 59.057%. In four post-hoc exact same-parent tests, FULL exceeded coordinate-basis, matched-spectrum, row-shuffled, and wrong-anatomy controls by 9.959, 9.698, 11.241, and 3.985 points, respectively (all 95% CIs excluded zero; Holm-adjusted P<0.001). A separate 60-participant same-paradigm evaluation retained a positive physical-operator contrast (+4.029 points; +2.338 to +5.773), whereas dynamic--static was inconclusive; its preregistered status is partial confirmation rather than unrestricted external validation. The SSM added +1.059 points (+0.013 to +1.892). Claims remain bounded to five binary motor-imagery domains and the tested operators.

Machine Learning.title: ThetreStageAI: Multi-View Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Bengali Theatre Production Planning
Machine Learning.summary: Staging a theatre performance requires coordinating dialogue, actor movement, stage directions, lighting focus, cue timing, and equipment constraints within the same production plan. This work presents ThetreStageAI, a retrieval augmented framework for structured Bengali theatre production planning. Rather than retrieving from one mixed corpus, the system maintains separate scene, actor-blocking, and lighting views. Bengali text is embedded with BGE-M3 and indexed in view-specific Qdrant collections. Retrieved references are combined with a production brief and passed to Gemini, which generates schema-constrained JSON containing characters, scenes, dialogue, stage directions, blocking, lighting, and optional sound cues. Structural and semantic checks are applied before acceptance, with at most one constrained repair attempt. We also construct a human-guided, LLM-assisted synthetic dataset of 500 short Bengali theatre records that expands to 1,500 retrieval documents. Dataset diagnostics confirm consistent identifiers and valid lighting fields while also revealing substantial dialogue repetition. A paired camera-ready evaluation compares single-combined and full multi-view retrieval under matched settings. The source code, dataset, and evaluation materials are publicly available.
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 12th IEEE International Conference on Sustainable Technologies and Engineering (IEEE iCOSTE 2026), Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 1-3, 2026

Machine Learning.title: Activation-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Sequence-Compressed Low-Rank Subspaces
Machine Learning.summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has become the standard approach for adapting large language models (LLMs). However, despite reducing trainable parameter counts, many PEFT methods remain memory-bound by token-level activation intermediates that scale linearly with sequence length, limiting their practicality for long-context and on-device adaptation. Unlike prior memory-efficient PEFT approaches that preserve token-level adapter activations, LARS (Low-memory Activation-Rank Subspace) reduces the sequence-length scaling of stored adapter activation intermediates from O(BSRL) to O(BRL) by performing adaptation within a sequence-level low-rank subspace. Through pooled feature extraction, low-rank subspace modulations, and residual projection, LARS reduces the overall memory footprint by 23% on GPUs and 47.8% on CPUs relative to LoRA at S = 1024, with relative savings increasing with context length. Experiments across reasoning, understanding, long-context, retrieval, and token-level tasks show that LARS maintains competitive performance relative to LoRA while substantially improving memory efficiency. Beyond GPUs, LARS also reduces average CPU power and energy consumption per optimisation step by 22.43% and 22.06%, respectively. These results demonstrate that activation-efficient adaptation provides a practical path toward resource-constrained and on-device fine-tuning of LLMs.

Machine Learning.title: The Sign Code: The Hidden Binary Nature of Deep Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Every neuron in a trained network outputs a number that can be separated into its sign (positive or negative) and its magnitude (absolute size). We call the set of all neuron signs the \textit{sign code}. This raises a key question: does classification depend more on the sign code or on the magnitudes? For overparameterized vision classifiers with sign-preserving activations, the answer is overwhelmingly the sign code. A $k$-nearest neighbor classifier operating only on this binary sign code achieves accuracy comparable to the full model across different architectures, activation functions, and datasets. Moreover, replacing all magnitudes in every layer with random noise while keeping the original signs barely changes residual network performance. In contrast, flipping just 20\% of the signs reduces accuracy to chance. Models generalize well when same-class inputs share similar sign codes. When this overlap is disrupted by a regularizer, training accuracy remains high, but test performance collapses. A margin decomposition helps explain these results: the sign-only contribution to each logit grows as $\sqrt{d}$ in network width, dominating the magnitude residual. The natural unit of analysis for these networks may not be through their continuous weight space but instead through their discrete sign codes.

Machine Learning.title: Trajectory-Triggered Sparse Collaborative Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Dense assistance methods such as speculative decoding repeatedly verify draft tokens with a target model, keeping target computation coupled to generation. We study sparse collaborative decoding, where a draft model generates most tokens and a target model is invoked only for short corrective segments. The key problem is deciding when to call the target. We show that local uncertainty is a weak trigger: entropy, negative log-likelihood, logit margin, top-$k$ mass, and velocity features give near-chance failure prediction, with AUC 0.50-0.53. In contrast, aggregate trajectory-shape features over the draft confidence path reach AUC 0.86 using a lightweight logistic predictor trained only from draft correctness labels. This induces a trigger-timing tradeoff: early calls have more leverage but weaker evidence, while later calls have stronger evidence but less ability to redirect the trajectory. Used online, learned sparse collaborative decoding improves over the best open-loop schedule by +5.3 to +20.0 accuracy points across five GSM8K draft-target pairs. On MATH-500, it gains 7.0-13.5 points when early prediction and target competence align, but loses when either is weak. On StrategyQA, it improves over open-loop by 5.0-8.3 points, showing transfer beyond arithmetics.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages. Accepted at the EMNLP 2026 uncertainty workshop

Machine Learning.title: How Many, but How Sure? Class Competition as a Confidence Proxy in Multi-Class Density-Based Counting
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-class density estimators can count objects in crowded scenes, but their class-wise outputs offer no indication of how reliably density mass has been allocated. We introduce a training-free confidence proxy based on local competition between the strongest class channels. The resulting prominence measure requires only the predicted density maps, with no retraining or access to model internals. We test whether residual competition is diagnostic of cross-class leakage by attenuating contested density at inference time. On DSACA predictions for the Hicks et al. dataset, this reduces overall MAE from 0.920 to 0.846, suggesting that class competition contains useful information about count reliability.
Machine Learning.comment: 2+1 pages, 1 figure; a 2027 Northern Lights Deep Learning Conference abstract

Machine Learning.title: When Magnitude Suffices: Reconstructing Time-Domain-Gated Microwave Signals Without Phase on a Thoracic Phantom
Machine Learning.summary: Time-domain gating separates the arrivals that form a microwave S-parameter measurement. It requires the measurement of complex values, so this application almost always uses a vector network analyzer (VNA). We show that, on one calibrated measurement configuration, the gated magnitude the VNA would give can be reconstructed from a magnitude-only sweep of a spectrum analyzer with a tracking generator (SA). We select the gate center for separability of the measured states, correct each instrument once by a per-bin subtraction of a reference state, and train a fully connected network on sweeps from both instruments. The test object is a torso phantom with lung-shaped compartments whose filling takes eleven dielectric states, each held out in turn. On $S_{11}$ the reconstruction from SA input reaches a shape error of 0.08 dB$^2$ with a state ordering of 0.81. This matches the reconstruction from VNA input. On $S_{21}$ it reaches 0.82 dB$^2$ and keeps the ordered groups of the states. An explicit phase prediction performs much worse, because gating needs the phase to about 0.2 rad RMS. Across eleven measurement configurations the dependence of phase on magnitude is strong for reflection and weak for transmission. This explains the difference between $S_{11}$ and $S_{21}$. Where the magnitude carries enough of the phase, a scalar instrument gives the gated response without any phase measurement after installation. On the open UM-BMID breast data set, with whole phantoms held out, the shape error of the network is 30 percent lower than that of a per-bin linear map.

Machine Learning.title: OrbiSim: World Models as Differentiable Physics Engines for Embodied Intelligence
Machine Learning.summary: We present OrbiSim, a novel robotic simulation paradigm that redefines world models as a fully differentiable physics engine for embodied intelligence. Unlike prior world models that focus on unconstrained imagination in latent or visual domains, OrbiSim establishes a unified, physically-grounded pathway that bridges structured scene assets, neural dynamics, and downstream reinforcement learning. By enabling end-to-end differentiability throughout the entire simulation loop -- spanning from explicit state transitions to visual observation generation -- OrbiSim supports tasks traditionally intractable for classical simulators, such as differentiable contact modeling, gradient-based policy optimization under sparse rewards, and intuitive physical inference. Empirical results demonstrate that OrbiSim significantly outperforms state-of-the-art world models in both predictive fidelity and control performance. Furthermore, its consistent responsiveness to asset configurations and physical parameters suggests its potential as a differentiable tool for enhancing robot simulation and policy training.

Machine Learning.title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.

Machine Learning.title: Empirical Bayesian Multi-Bandit Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-task learning in contextual bandits has attracted significant research interest due to its potential to enhance decision-making across multiple related tasks by leveraging shared structures and task-specific heterogeneity. In this article, we propose a novel hierarchical Bayesian framework for learning in various bandit instances. This framework captures both the heterogeneity and the correlations among different bandit instances through a hierarchical Bayesian model, enabling effective information sharing while accommodating instance-specific variations. Unlike previous methods that overlook the learning of the covariance structure across bandits, we introduce an empirical Bayesian approach to estimate the covariance matrix of the prior distribution. This enhances both the practicality and flexibility of learning across multi-bandits. Building on this approach, we develop two efficient algorithms: ebmTS (Empirical Bayesian Multi-Bandit Thompson Sampling) and ebmUCB (Empirical Bayesian Multi-Bandit Upper Confidence Bound), both of which incorporate the estimated prior into the decision-making process. We provide the frequentist regret upper bounds for the proposed algorithms, thereby filling a research gap in the field of multi-bandit problems. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithms, particularly in complex environments. Our methods achieve lower cumulative regret compared to existing techniques, highlighting their effectiveness in balancing exploration and exploitation across multi-bandits.

Machine Learning.title: Exploration and Experimentation with a Misspecified Simulator
Machine Learning.summary: Randomized experiments are the standard for measuring causal effects that guide decisions, but are costly. Simulators calibrated to historical data offer a cheaper alternative, but their policies can become suboptimal under drift, a change in dynamics after calibration. We study if, when, and how to collect data for recalibrating the simulator. We consider a system with multiple units running in parallel and managed by a single operator. The real-world system is a partially observed process with a latent variable, while the simulator models it as a fully observed Markovian process, and thus is misspecified. Two data collection strategies exploit the current policy: (i) never recalibrating and (ii) recalibrating from on-policy data (passive adaptation). Two others collect off-policy data by trying actions outside the current policy: (iii) continuous exploration across all units and (iv) randomized experimentation on a sample of units over a predefined window. We investigate these strategies theoretically and in a vending-machine simulation. Experiments can improve on passive adaptation when drift is invisible in on-policy data or recalibration lags behind continuing drift. Experimentation is preferable to exploration when trying a worse action is expensive and the dynamics may not have changed.

Machine Learning.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
Machine Learning.summary: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.

Machine Learning.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
Machine Learning.summary: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.

Machine Learning.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
Machine Learning.summary: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent work has constructed anytime-valid envelopes that do, but deterministic envelopes are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each coupling a specific algorithm to a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for constructing such anytime-valid data-adaptive boundaries for a large class of iterative algorithms. Performance measures of many of these algorithms satisfy a one-step recursion that reduces the entire error analysis to a single general requirement: time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. We formalize this through a strongly adapted sub-$ψ$ condition, and derive off-the-shelf boundary constructions via continuous and discrete mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. We show how these boundaries can be directly coupled with a separate algorithmic analysis that derives the one-step recursion to provide a class of readymade anytime-valid envelopes across diverse settings including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), temporal difference learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD. In particular, for SGD, our framework either recovers or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Expected Values: Risk-Sensitive Planning with Distributional Monte-Carlo Tree Search
Machine Learning.summary: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) typically stores only scalar mean estimates, which makes it poorly suited for tail-risk objectives such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR). We introduce Categorical Thompson Sampling with Optimism (CATSO) and Particle Thompson Sampling with Optimism (PATSO), two distributional MCTS algorithms that maintain finite-support empirical backup laws at Q-edges. CATSO represents Q-edge laws with categorical atoms and Dirichlet Thompson sampling, while PATSO represents them with adaptive particles. Both algorithms select actions using the CVaR of a Thompson-sampled Q-edge law plus a polynomial optimism bonus, and propagate scalar continuation values through visit-weighted averages of child Q-edge CVaR scores. For the finite-depth nested CVaR planning target, we prove an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the root value error after $n$ rollouts, which upper-bounds the risk-sensitive simple regret. CATSO adds a fixed-grid discretization bias, while capped PATSO adds a tunable Wasserstein compression bias. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show that distributional Q-edges improve lower-tail return and reduce catastrophic outcomes when mean-optimal and risk-sensitive behavior differ.
Machine Learning.comment: Proceedings of the 40th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems

Machine Learning.title: Can Graph Learning Learn Circuits?
Machine Learning.summary: Circuit localization is a mechanistic interpretability task whose goal is to identify a sparse subgraph of a transformer's computation graph sufficient to reproduce a particular behavior. Most established methods localize circuits independently for each model-task pair. We instead frame circuit localization as a graph machine learning problem in which the edges of a computation graph represent computational pathways, and graph neural networks (GNNs) model interactions among these pathways. We introduce Graph Circuit Learning (GCL), a supervised, amortized framework that trains a GNN across multiple model-task pairs and applies it to unseen cases. To provide sufficient data, we augment the InterpBench benchmark with additional cases derived from TracrBench programs. Of the 46 evaluated GCL configurations, the one selected by cross-validation scored a median edge AUROC of 0.946 (interquartile interval [0.841, 0.980]) on the 16 held-out cases of our evaluation split. Removing all message-passing edges reduces the median to 0.926. We also adapt PGExplainer, a GNN explainability method, to circuit localization, obtaining a median edge AUROC of 0.950 on the same cases. These preliminary results suggest that graph machine learning offers a natural and potentially powerful perspective on circuit localization, one we hope encourages closer exchange between the two communities.
Machine Learning.comment: Oral presentation at the Fifth Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG 2026), Extended Abstract Track

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Latent Personalization: Integrating HRV-Conditioned Personalization via LLM for Interpretable Stress Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Stress detection based on heart rate variability (HRV) has received increasing attention. However, existing personalized approaches integrate personal attributes with HRV through latent representations, limiting the interpretability of their interactions. In this work, we propose an LLM-enhanced personalized stress detection framework that integrates HRV features and personal attributes through LLM-based semantic interpretation. The proposed framework achieves a 29.9% relative MCC improvement over the strongest baseline on TILES-2018 while providing human-readable descriptions of individual physiological responses. The results highlight the potential of LLM-based semantic interpretation for achieving both effective and interpretable personalized stress detection.

Machine Learning.title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs
Machine Learning.summary: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.

Machine Learning.title: BenthicDINO: Physics-Informed Self-Distillation for View-Invariant Side-Scan Sonar Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Automated interpretation of side-scan sonar (SSS) imagery is traditionally hindered by view-dependence, as recorded intensities inextricably conflate intrinsic seabed reflectivity with transient acquisition geometries and acoustic artifacts. To address this, we introduce BenthicDINO, a physics-informed self-supervised learning framework that decouples acquisition dynamics from seabed representations. Utilizing a ConvNeXt-v2 backbone, physics-guided augmentations, and an HSIC penalty, BenthicDINO explicitly enforces feature invariance to physical viewing parameters like slant range and incidence angle. Evaluations demonstrate exceptional data efficiency - achieving near-peak performance in benthic habitat mapping with only 10% of available labels - and strong cross-domain generalization, outperforming fully supervised baselines on the AI4Shipwrecks benchmark using frozen representations.

Machine Learning.title: Out of Support, Not Out of Reach: In-Context Learning with Unsupported Instructions and Composed Tasks
Machine Learning.summary: In-Context Learning (ICL) enables pretrained LLMs to adapt to downstream tasks from a small set of input-output demonstrations, without parameter updates. Yet existing theory primarily explains ICL as identifying a latent task already represented in pretraining, leaving unclear whether ICL can succeed when either the instruction or the target task falls outside the pretraining support. We develop a theoretical framework under mild assumptions that separates these two forms of distribution shift. For target tasks represented in pretraining, we show that demonstrations can identify the task and reduce sensitivity to pretrain-supported prompt templates as their number increases. For an unsupported instruction, we show that under a fixed model-induced reference extension, demonstration evidence can dominate an $N$-independent instruction shift while preserving the exponential identification rate. We then use the same ICL framework as an interpretive lens for long-horizon target tasks that are not represented in pretraining but admit a plan that decomposes them into pretraining-supported subtasks. Applying the supported-task analysis step by step yields a standard accumulated-error bound and clarifies how invoking familiar subtasks along an intermediate-state trajectory can avoid directly selecting the unsupported complete task. Together, our results characterize when demonstrations, instructions, and task decomposition can support ICL beyond the corresponding pretraining supports.

Machine Learning.title: Interpreting SSL Representations for Spoof Detection: a WavLM Study
Machine Learning.summary: Self-supervised speech models such as WavLM achieve strong spoofing detection performance, yet which layers encode the most spoof-relevant information and what acoustic properties they capture remain opaque. We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM using the ASVspoof 5 database, combining three complementary analyses: (i) per-layer linear probing with attack-level evaluation across speech synthesis, voice conversion, and adversarial attacks; (ii) a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) linking layer representations to spoofing-relevant acoustic features; (iii) an exhaustive grid search over layer subsets showing that use of five layers outperforms full thirteen-layer pooling. CCA analysis reveals that, while most acoustic features peak in alignment with mid-layers and then decay, voice quality measures jitter, shimmer, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio show the opposite trend, with correlation increasing toward later layers. Embedding visualisations reveal that deeper layers capture a continuous acoustic similarity among attacks rather than discrete categories, suggesting these layers encode fundamental synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures.
Machine Learning.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Published at IWBF 2026. An extended abstract of this work was presented as a poster at Odyssey 2026

Machine Learning.title: Leaner Transformers Can Easily Learn to Cluster
Machine Learning.summary: Transformers have in-context learning capabilities, where some known learning algorithms can be executed in the forward pass through the model. Recent work shows that transformers can exactly perform Lloyd's algorithm for $k$-means clustering with $n$ points in $d$ dimensions with an embedding size $d_{\textsf{emb}} = d+k$ (thus, requiring attention projection matrices of size $(d+k)^2$). In this work, we build upon this result in the following ways: First, we present an equally expressive but smaller transformer that executes Lloyd's algorithm with embedding size $d_{\textsf{emb}} = (d + \lceil \log_2 k \rceil)$. Next, we train these transformers to learn the clustering algorithms given a distribution of clustering tasks, and theoretically characterize and empirically validate the factors affecting the convergence and in-distribution generalization of learning algorithms based on stochastic gradients. Finally, we probe the general clustering abilities of these learned algorithms (in the form of transformers), and try to understand situations where they succeed and fail.

Machine Learning.title: Uncertainty-aware AI-enabled framework for predicting hydrogen dispersion in confined spaces to enhance operator situational awareness
Machine Learning.summary: We present a two-stage AI-enabled framework for enhancing operator situational awareness during compressed hydrogen bunkering in maritime confined spaces. In the event of a leak, the framework first estimates the unknown leakage rate from early sensor readings and then forecasts how the hydrogen cloud will disperse over the next time steps, providing operators with a predicted concentration map together with confidence bounds. The framework is based on two independent AI models building one AI system. The AI system is designed as a decision-support tool. It augments sensor readings, and thus enhances operator situational awareness and supports decision-making. This enables preventive safety barriers to be deployed before hazardous concentrations are reached, while an independent emergency shutdown system remains the ultimate safety layer. The system design incorporates safeguards to ensure the AI system operates within its competence envelope. Trained and tested on an open dataset of confined-space hydrogen releases, the framework achieves a mean absolute error of $0.052$~g/s in leakage-rate estimation and $\approx0.018$ in hydrogen-concentration prediction, approaching the sensor precision bound of $\pm0.01$. The hydrogen-concentration prediction provides well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that allow operators to judge the reliability of each forecast. These results suggest that the framework may provide early information about hazardous concentration build-up, potentially supporting preventive actions by operators.
Machine Learning.comment: Submitted to Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries

Machine Learning.title: Adaptive conformal prediction on the Grassmannian
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce a conformal prediction framework for regression with Grassmann-valued responses. The proposed method constructs prediction regions in the form of metric balls directly on the Grassmann manifold, using basis-invariant geometric distances as non-conformity measures and scaling the corresponding non-conformity scores through a learned prediction difficulty estimator. This yields locally adaptive, input-dependent prediction regions that respect the underlying manifold geometry, while retaining the finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction under exchangeability. We evaluate several Grassmannian distance metrics and compare their prediction-region efficiency on synthetic benchmarks and an airfoil inverse shape-design problem. The results highlight the advantages of geometry-aware non-conformity scores, while local adaptation improves empirical coverage uniformity across prediction difficulty levels and, in strongly heteroscedastic settings, can substantially reduce prediction-region size while maintaining the target coverage.

Machine Learning.title: Graph Transductive Sharpening: Leveraging Unlabeled Predictions in Node Classification
Machine Learning.summary: In the transductive setting, where the full graph is observed but node labels are only partially available, progress in semi-supervised node classification has largely focused on architectural innovation. In this paper, we revisit an orthogonal axis: the training objective. We start from a simple observation: transductive models produce predictions for every node during training, including nodes without labels. These unlabeled-node predictions may contain useful training signal, but standard supervised objectives discard them because no ground-truth labels are available. Inspired by the decomposition of cross-entropy into a label-dependent alignment term and a label-independent entropy term, we propose prediction confidence as a natural way to extract this signal in the absence of labels. This motivates Transductive Sharpening (TS): a loss-level modification that minimizes prediction entropy on unlabeled nodes while counterbalancing this effect on labeled nodes. We evaluate Transductive Sharpening across a wide range of node-classification benchmarks and observe consistent performance improvements without requiring any changes to the backbone architecture. Code is available at https://github.com/transductive-sharpening/tunedGNN.

Machine Learning.title: Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model
Machine Learning.summary: Nonstationarity and heterogeneous dynamics are common in financial and macroeconomic time series. Volatility alternates between calm and turbulent regimes, interest rates follow monetary-policy cycles, and major events trigger persistent structural shifts. We propose the Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model (TPGPMM), a Bayesian nonparametric framework for regime identification and nonstationary prediction that infers such regimes and their within-regime dependence from data, without Markovian assumptions. It combines (i) an adaptive Pitman-Yor process prior on ordered compositions, mapped to block lengths with contiguity enforced by construction, and (ii) regime-specific Gaussian processes for temporal dependence, yielding a nonstationary predictive distribution. By inferring its discount parameter, the prior adapts to homogeneous and highly heterogeneous regime lengths. Unlike sequential or Markov-switching methods, it flags persistent structural shifts as change points rather than reacting to transient shocks. A split-merge Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with exact Gibbs updates of regime boundaries jointly learns change points and hyperparameters in batch, quantifying uncertainty over the partition and within-regime dynamics. With an RBF kernel and a fixed, data-informed noise level, TPGPMM produces a sparse, confident segmentation. On simulated data it recovers the true regimes, and on the CBOE Volatility Index and the 10-year US Treasury yield it identifies regimes aligned with documented market and monetary-policy events. For prediction, variants estimating the noise level fit better than change-point baselines and fit and forecast better than the main specification, at the cost of a less sparse or less event-aligned segmentation; with a regime mean, they fit better than a fitted stationary Gaussian process and have lower forecast RMSE except at the shortest horizons.

Machine Learning.title: Cross-Dialect Generalization Without Retraining: Benchmarks and Evaluation of Schema-Derived Constrained Decoding for MLIR
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) underlies modern ML compiler infrastructure (TensorFlow, JAX/StableHLO, PyTorch Inductor, IREE), yet appears only in trace amounts in code-LM pretraining corpora. MLIR is also extensible by design: new dialects ship per application domain, so a fine-tuned model per dialect does not scale. We ask whether inference-time priors derived mechanically from each dialect's Operation Definition Specification (ODS) can substitute for gradient-based adaptation. First, we release four natural-language-to-MLIR benchmarks across three dialects (MLIR-Spec-150, Linalg-Spec-30, StableHLO-Spec-30, StableHLO-Held-Out-200), totaling 410 in-scope NL-to-MLIR pairs, plus a 25-program out-of-grammar stress set, with functional references on 30 Spec prompts, under Apache-2.0 with Gebru datasheets and Croissant 1.1 metadata. Second, we build a three-layer schema-derived constraint stack: a CFG over op signatures (C1), type-domain splits from an ODS-extracted type lattice (C2), and an SSA-scope validator driving five-retry rejection sampling (C3). Porting it to StableHLO required no new constraint-layer code. On structurally dominated dialects, SmolLM2-1.7B with token-level constraints matches or exceeds 15B-34B code LMs running post-hoc rejection at a matched retry budget and 8-25x the per-generation speed: on linalg it reaches 80.0% verify-valid (three runs, n=125), 21 to 44 pp above CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B with non-overlapping CIs. The comparison is between systems, not models: under the baselines' post-hoc protocol, SmolLM2 falls from 52.0% to 24.5% on arith+func. On arith+func and the templated StableHLO-Held-Out-200 the baselines match or beat the SLM; we scope these as non-win cells. We release benchmarks, decoder, every per-prompt generation, and a pinned reproducibility Dockerfile.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track; camera-ready version. 31 pages (10 main + references + appendix + checklist). Code: https://github.com/plawanrath/slm-to-mlir-constrained-emitter Datasets: https://huggingface.co/collections/plawanrath/cross-dialect-mlir-benchmarks-neurips-2026-e-and-d

Machine Learning.title: Missing value imputation with adversarial random forests - MissARF
Machine Learning.summary: Handling missing values is a common challenge in biostatistical analyses, typically addressed by imputation methods. We propose a novel, fast, and easy-to-use imputation method called missing value imputation with adversarial random forests (MissARF), based on generative machine learning, that provides both single and multiple imputation. MissARF employs adversarial random forest (ARF) for density estimation and data synthesis. To impute a missing value of an observation, we condition on the non-missing values and sample from the estimated conditional distribution generated by ARF. Our experiments demonstrate that MissARF performs comparably to state-of-the-art single and multiple imputation methods in terms of imputation quality and fast runtime with no additional costs for multiple imputation.

Machine Learning.title: A Topological Signature of Learning under Noisy Labels
Machine Learning.summary: How does noisy supervision change the representations learned by a neural network? Training accuracy measures agreement with training labels but provides little information about representation geometry. We use persistent homology to track loop structure across distance thresholds in neural activations. Experiments span image classification, text classification, and modular arithmetic. On a fixed CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 training probe, equally sized clean-label and corrupted-label subsets show no detectable persistence difference at epoch 10, whereas corrupted-label subsets have higher persistence at epoch 50. The contrast survives uniform-scale controls, even though predictions match the assigned noisy labels for only 7-11% of corrupted probe examples at that checkpoint. Normalisation preserves the crossover between clean and noisy training trajectories on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, whereas CIFAR-100/ResNet-18 shows no crossover under any of the five evaluated constructions. In a separate noise-rate calibration comparison across five pipelines, mean activation norm achieves a higher mean in-sample R2 than raw persistence (0.936 versus 0.908). These findings show that noisy supervision leaves a measurable geometric signature even when agreement with corrupted labels is low. Comparing persistence under scale controls with label-fitting measurements offers a way to study how representations respond to label corruption beyond what training accuracy reveals.

Machine Learning.title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning
Machine Learning.summary: We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost $Δ$. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.

Machine Learning.title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
Machine Learning.summary: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality--diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

Machine Learning.title: Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts, and tokens. We investigate whether network topology can identify transaction methods that describe DeFi operations. We extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.
Machine Learning.comment: 24 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables, 25 references 15th International Conference on Complex Networks and Their Applications

Machine Learning.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the BabyLM Workshop at EMNLP 2026

Machine Learning.title: RamanBench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Machine Learning on Raman Spectroscopy
Machine Learning.summary: Machine learning (ML) has transformed many scientific fields, yet key applications still lack standardized benchmarks. Raman spectroscopy, a widely used technique for non-invasive molecular analysis, is one such field where progress is limited by fragmented datasets, inconsistent evaluation, and models that fail to capture the structure of spectral data. We introduce RamanBench, the first large-scale, fully reproducible benchmark for ML on Raman spectroscopy, consisting of streamlined data access (https://pypi.org/project/raman-data/), evaluation protocols and code (https://pypi.org/project/raman-bench/), as well as a live leaderboard (https://huggingface.co/spaces/HTW-KI-Werkstatt/RamanBench). It unifies 77 datasets (including 17 first released with this benchmark) across four domains, comprising 325,862 spectra and spanning classification and regression tasks under diverse experimental conditions. We benchmark 28 models under a standardized protocol, including classical methods (e.g., PLS), Raman-specific (e.g., RamanNet), tabular foundation models (TFMs; e.g., TabPFN), and time-series approaches (e.g., ROCKET). TFMs consistently outperform domain-specific and gradient boosting baselines, while time-series models remain competitive. However, no single method dominates across these heterogeneous datasets, revealing that Raman spectroscopy remains an open challenge for machine learning. Therefore, we invite the community to contribute new approaches to our living benchmark, with the potential to accelerate advances in critical applications such as medical diagnostics, biological research, and materials science.

Machine Learning.title: Predictable Scaling: Efficient Model Exploration via Scaling-Law Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Evaluating candidate changes (hypotheses) to recommendation models requires full-scale training runs consuming thousands of GPU-hours, severely limiting the hypothesis space engineers can feasibly explore. We introduce Predictable Scaling (PS), a systematic framework that exploits empirically verified regularity conditions to predict full-scale model performance from small-scale proxies. PS constructs scaled-down variants via composable scaling functions along distinct resource axes, and projects metrics to the target scale via curve fitting with calibrated uncertainty estimates. We compare three prediction strategies of increasing expressiveness: even the simplest (raw proxy) achieves prediction error within the empirical noise floor of repeated-run variance; the most expressive (Gaussian Process) provides an indicative 15% relative MAE improvement and calibrated uncertainty. Evaluation on two ranking models of increasing complexity---a task-specific model and a foundation model---demonstrates that PS correctly ranks actionable hypotheses across diverse hypothesis types at 79-88% compute reductions.

Machine Learning.title: Regularized free deconvolution for spectral repair of resampling distortion in high-dimensional particle filters
Machine Learning.summary: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre-resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre-registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
Machine Learning.comment: This is a preprint of an article submitted to Signal Processing (Elsevier). The implementation and experiment scripts are available at https://github.com/songming-teaching/spectral-repair-resampling. This is the second paper in a series on spectral analysis of particle filters. The first paper is available at arXiv:2610.16680

Machine Learning.title: RECREG: Recovery-based Shielding for Regular Safety Properties in Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: In many real-world scenarios we need to consider formal requirements, such as safety and constraint compliance, to deploy Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. In this paper we introduce RecReg, a safe RL framework capable of enforcing non-Markovian regular safety properties via recovery-based shielding. RecReg is a unified approach that supports different levels of a priori knowledge and safety guarantees. The paper primarily focuses on building the theoretical foundations for RecReg in the tabular setting, providing rigorous safety and convergence guarantees that are not present in related work. We provide an extensive set of empirical results using the MASA-Safe-RL library, and we outline an extension of RecReg to deep RL domains using SOTA model-based RL. Our empirical results demonstrate that RecReg achieves efficient learning and matches the theory in this paper.
